text: The matrix and conflict versions resolve at sign-in and stay with the session until it ends, and the resolved role set, scope and the two version labels are handed to gateway-bff for its Redis session record while rwb-access keeps no session table of its own.
why: The legacy story kept the versions on the session object and refused to change them under an open session, and the target forbids a session table and a token store in a service; without a stated home the AC9 behaviour cannot be built.
read: RWB-E1-022 section 8 BR7 and section 13 build step 8; Architecture v5 Text Extract v1 slides 20 (gateway-bff: Redis sessions only) and 35; ADR-010; RWB-PLT-N006-INF
confirm: rwb-access service owner and the edge owner at the wave 1 design gate
impact: Decides where the version labels live; adds no table, no column and no schema to rwb_access and keeps the sessions in the edge store

text: A role conflict refuses the session with MSG-P4-006 naming the pair, and the refusal and the incident it raises are one refusal fact with reason code ROLE_CONFLICT.
why: The legacy criterion requires an incident on the security administrator queue, and no source of the read set names an incident operation, a queue or a target service, so the refusal fact is the only channel that exists.
read: RWB-E1-022 section 5 X4 and section 7 AC6; Architecture v5 Text Extract v1 slide 14 (P4 publishes no event); RWB-P4-E1039-APP's access-entry writer
confirm: Security administrator role owner and the audit owner at the wave 1 design gate
impact: Gives the incident an addressee through the record that already exists; a dedicated incident operation would be a new contract and is not created

text: An unmapped or inactive group gives no role, and its name is written on the sign-in fact as a group name only, never as a person's attribute.
why: The ownership and the FSD agree that a group with no active role row confers nothing, and the legacy criterion also requires the unmapped name to be visible, so the fact must carry a name whose kind has to be fixed to keep personal data out.
read: RWB-E1-022 section 5 X6, section 8 BR1 and section 7 AC8; FSD P4 v3 AC-EXC-P4-001-04; Architecture v5 Text Extract v1 slide 35
confirm: rwb-access service owner at the wave 1 design gate
impact: The fact carries a group name and a reference; no person attribute reaches a log or an event

text: rwb-access caches nothing of another service's data: the reference values and the team and region codes are read per call through the rwb-case contracts, and no row is copied into rwb_access.
why: The reference lists and the teams are P3's under the ownership map, and a copy in rwb_access would be a second source that drifts at the first version change; the schema story states that no object of rwb_access references rwb_case.
read: Ownership Map v1 (lov_value, reference_row, reference_version, queue, queue_member owned by P3); DP-01 and DP-07; RWB-PLT-E1043-CON and RWB-P3-E1043-CON; RWB-P3-E1019-CON
confirm: rwb-access service owner and the rwb-case service owner at the wave 1 contract freeze
impact: One hop per resolution for the values and the team codes; no local copy, no local invalidation and no drift

text: The sign-in and refusal facts are written locally by the access-entry writer of RWB-P4-E1039-APP and published to rwb.decision-record.v1; this story supplies the reference, the area, the right, the result and the reason code and builds no writer of its own.
why: The access log is written locally and published to the decision topic, and the writer is one story of this service; a second writer inside the resolver would duplicate the record path and the hash chain.
read: Architecture v5 Text Extract v1 slides 20 (every service writes its own decision records) and 22; DP-03; RWB-PLT-E1027-CON; RWB-E1-022 section 13 build step 5
confirm: rwb-access service owner and the audit owner at the wave 1 design gate
impact: One record path for every refusal and sign-in; the resolver adds no writer, no table and no topic

text: The two operations of the access contract are published at POST /api/recovery/access/v1/authorise and GET /api/recovery/access/v1/me/permissions, built from the operation names of Architecture v5 slide 14 and the base rule of section R4.
why: The slide names the operations and the Ownership Map has no path row for either, so the base rule is the only published derivation of a path; leaving it open would leave every consumer guessing the same two strings.
read: Architecture v5 Text Extract v1 slides 14 and 41; Template and Rules section R4 and DP-13; Ownership Map v1 api list (no row for authorise or me/permissions)
confirm: Contract owner of rwb-access and the platform edge owner at the contract freeze
impact: Fixes two paths and no payload; a later Ownership Map path row would replace the assumption and not the operations

text: The authorise request carries the role codes of the resolved session, the scope type with the team and region codes, the capability area, the right and the delegation band key of the action, and the answer carries the decision, the matrix version, the conflict version and on a refusal the reason code and the message id.
why: No source fixes the payload: the legacy contract was a Java method over a SessionContext type and the slide names only the inputs role, scope and DoA, so the contract must state the shape it publishes and say that it is stated.
read: RWB-E1-022 section 12; Architecture v5 Text Extract v1 slide 14 (POST /authorise: role, scope, DoA) and slide 11 (REST, one hop, 2 s); TSD P4 v3 T-A.2 API-P4-012 (the resolved session holds roles, scope, matrix and conflict versions)
applied_in: RWB-P4-E1022-CON sections 4, 7 AC2 and AC3, and 12.1
confirm: Contract owner of rwb-access with the consuming squads at the contract freeze
impact: Fixes the shape every consumer compiles against; it carries identifiers and version labels only and no business value

text: The grantee of schema rwb_access is a login named rwb_access, following the one-login-per-service pattern of section R4 and Architecture v5 slide 29, and the platform DB story sets its real name, its password and its connection pool.
why: Section R4 fixes one login per service and no source fixes the P4 login name; the grant script, the boundary check and the rollback all need a named grantee to be testable.
read: Template and Rules section R4 (login per service); Architecture v5 Text Extract v1 slide 29 (one login per service, rwb_case shown as the pattern); RWB-PLT-N011-DB (pools, migrator role and grant check)
applied_in: RWB-P4-E1022-DB sections 3, 7 AC1 and AC7, 13 and 17
confirm: ACE DBA and the platform DB owner at the wave 1 schema gate
impact: Names the grantee of the script only; no credential appears in a migration, a story or a runbook

text: The role-to-group mapping rows stay in role.entra_group as TSD P4 v3 defines them, the ACE group facts behind a mapping are read only through the P1 contract or RWB-P1-E1069-APP, and no object of rwb_access names an ACE schema, the recovery schema or public.
why: FSD P4 v3 reads the mapping from v_ace_iam_group while TSD P4 v3 defines role.entra_group and the mapping contract keeps the rows in the table; R-PREC puts the technical specification above the functional one, and the boundary rule forbids a service reading ACE directly.
read: FSD P4 v3 A2.1 field catalog; TSD P4 v3 T3.1 role (DF-REF-039); Template and Rules section R3 R-PREC items 6 and 7; Ownership Map v1 role row; RWB-P1-E1069-APP (the ACE view owner)
confirm: P4 service owner, the P1 data owner and the architecture review at the wave 1 schema gate
impact: Keeps one mapping row set in rwb_access and one read path for the ACE facts; no view, synonym or grant crosses the schema boundary

text: outbox_event, processed_event and idempotency_key are created in rwb_access from the event platform template published by RWB-PLT-TE006-CON, unchanged, by this service's own database story.
why: The ownership map keeps the three objects with PLT as library objects created in every service schema and Architecture v5 slide 29 forbids a cross-schema write, so this schema must hold them before the service can publish or consume idempotently.
read: Ownership Map v1 rows outbox_event, processed_event and idempotency_key (owner PLT, asm ASM-A6-tables-8); Architecture v5 Text Extract v1 slides 11 and 20; RWB-PLT-TE006-CON
confirm: ACE DBA and the event platform owner at the wave 1 schema gate
impact: The three objects are applied from one template and no column is invented here; a template change is one change in one place

text: A matrix version and a masking version resolve at sign-in and stay until the session ends, so open work keeps the version it signed in under and a new version answers only new sessions.
why: The legacy flow step 5 keeps open sessions on their version and RWB-E1-022 resolves the version at sign-in; no source states the rule for the split service.
read: Legacy RWB-E1-037 section 4 step 5; FSD P4 A2.4; RWB-P4-E1022-APP
confirm: Solution architect with the access owner
impact: A withdrawn permission stays in force for the life of an open session, up to the session timeout; the alternative is a per-request resolve, which costs one read per call.

text: A person whose roles include both halves of a role_conflict row at the conflict version in force is refused the session, and the refusal is recorded with reason ROLE_CONFLICT.
why: The separation-of-duty rule is in the legacy story and the sources give no other enforcement point; the session is the earliest point at which the pair can be seen.
read: Legacy RWB-E1-019 BR9 and section 10; FSD P4 AC-EXC-P4-001-03; TSD P4 v3 T3.1 role_conflict
applied_in: RWB-P4-E1037-APP sections 2 and 9; RWB-P4-E1037-CON sections 8 and 9
confirm: Security administrator
impact: A mistaken entitlement blocks the person at sign-in instead of being discovered in an audit, and the incident queue carries the pair.

text: An Entra ID group that maps to no Workbench role, or to an inactive role, gives the person no role at all and no default.
why: Default deny is the architecture rule and no source defines a fallback role; a fallback would grant rights nobody approved.
read: Architecture v5 slides 10 and 35; legacy MSG-P4-001
confirm: Security architecture reviewer
impact: A person with one unmapped group of several keeps the roles of the mapped groups and is refused 401 only when no group maps.

text: rwb-access caches no data of another service and no answer of a peer: the version in force is read from rwb_access on each call, and only the platform library caches the policy answer in the consuming service.
why: P4 owns the policy rows, so a local cache adds a staleness window with no gain, and the sources give no cache to the access owner.
read: Architecture v5 slide 20 (cache in the consuming service); slide 14 (rwb-access is the reference-data owner)
confirm: Service owner
impact: Each read costs one query on rwb_access inside the 2 s budget; a policy change is visible to a new session at once.

text: The access log is written locally through the decision-record library to rwb.decision-record.v1 and the central ledger stays with P7; a refused call is passed to the access-entry writer of RWB-P4-E1039-APP, which P4 owns and which writes no P7 table.
why: DP-03 moves the decision log to a local library plus the shared topic, and the access log is a P4 object that must be written without a P7 table write.
read: Template and Rules §R5.5 DP-03; Ownership Map (decision_log_entry is P7); Architecture v5 slide 14 (access log in rwb_access)
confirm: Solution architect
impact: The access query reads the local ledger copy and the central search is P7's operation; a P4 search over a P7 table is not built.

text: The membership refresh interval is five minutes, read from the parameter rwb.access.membership-refresh-minutes=5, so a leaver's session ends at the first request after the refresh.
why: The legacy story assumes the interval (DL38) and no source fixes a value; the parameter keeps it changeable without a build.
read: Legacy RWB-E1-037 section 4 step 11, section 13 and AC8; DL38
confirm: Security administrator
impact: A leaver keeps access for at most five minutes after the group is removed; a shorter value costs more group reads, a longer one widens the window.

text: This service keeps the load and approve operations for its own permission and masking tables, while the generic reference-load path for lists, queues, timers, templates and parameters stays with rwb-case.
why: API Specification v4 gives the two operations x-module P4 and TSD P4 v3 T-A names them, while the R-PREC default ruling gives generic reference data to P3; the split is the only reading that keeps both sources.
read: API Specification v4 x-module P4 for /admin/reference-loads and /admin/reference-loads/{loadId}/approve; TSD P4 v3 API-P4-005 and API-P4-006; Template and Rules §R3 default rulings
confirm: Solution architect with the P3 and P4 owners
impact: One gateway route answers two owners unless the two path sets are separated; a merge of the two stories into one owner would move the permission load out of P4.

text: The 756 permission rows of AC1 stand as 54 roles against 14 capability areas, and the roster of TSD P4 v3 T6.1 (42 role codes) grows to 54 by go-live; no row count, role count or area count is a code constant.
why: The legacy criteria count 756 rows and the FSD takes version PM-2026.12 into effect with 756 rows, while the TSD roster lists 42 role codes; the file is the source of the count either way.
read: Legacy RWB-E1-037 AC1 and section 2; FSD P4 A2.1 and A2.4; TSD P4 v3 T6.1
confirm: Security administrator with the solution architect
impact: A version with 42 roles holds 588 rows and fails the legacy count until the roster is completed; the loader must count the file, never a constant.

text: GET /api/recovery/access/v1/masking-policies is the base rule of §R4 applied to the operation Arch v5 slide 14 names, and it answers under Reference data R.
why: Slide 14 names the operation and the service base is fixed by §R4, while the API Specification v4, TSD P4 v3 T-A and the Ownership Map give it no path and no right.
read: Architecture v5 slide 14; Template and Rules §R4 and §R5.5 DP-13; API Specification v4 (no masking-policies path); Ownership Map (no path row)
applied_in: RWB-P4-E1037-CON sections 2 and 12.1; RWB-P4-E1037-APP sections 11 and 12.1
confirm: Solution architect and the API owner
impact: A different path or right breaks the consumer's generated client and needs a new API Specification row; the answer shape is unaffected.

text: rwb.access.AccessPolicyChanged.v1 carries the change kind (matrix or masking), the version label, the effective date and the approver reference, and never a field value, a person, a case id or a letter of a role.
why: Arch v5 slide 14 names the event and fixes no payload; the data-minimisation rule of NFR-040 and the no-personal-data rule of slide 35 fix what it may not carry.
read: Architecture v5 slide 14 and slide 35; NFR-040; RWB-PLT-E1037-CON AC3 and AC5
confirm: Solution architect with the event platform owner
impact: A consumer that needs more than the version label must call the matrix read; a richer payload would carry policy data over the topic.

text: The rwb_access baseline objects role, permission, masking_rule, role_conflict and delegation_limit are created by the service template migration V0001 of RWB-PLT-E1044-CON, and this legacy key adds only its two unique indexes, because WP B-P4-01 carries no DB story for RWB-E1-037.
why: The service template owns the schema baseline and every service has its own DB story; this key has none in the WP, so the baseline cannot be left unowned.
read: Template and Rules §R5.5 DP-15 and §R5.7; TSD P4 v3 T3.1; WP B-P4-01 write list (no DB story for RWB-E1-037)
applied_in: RWB-P4-E1037-APP sections 3 and 13; RWB-P4-E1037-CON sections 3 and 12.7
confirm: ACE DB team with the service owner
impact: If the baseline does not carry the five tables, the index migration fails and a DB story of this key must be created before the first load.

text: GET /api/recovery/access/v1/admin/roles is one path with one contract; RWB-P4-E1019-APP answers the role code, class, default scope and conflict fields and RWB-P4-E1037-APP answers the permission rows and the matrix version of the same answer.
why: The Ownership Map gives P4 one path and the TSD gives it one purpose (list roles with permissions and scope), so two slices contribute fields to one operation instead of publishing two paths.
read: Ownership Map (GET /admin/roles is P4); TSD P4 v3 API-P4-007; API Specification v4 /admin/roles x-module P4; RWB-P4-E1019-APP
confirm: Solution architect with both app owners
impact: Two answers on one path would break the generated client; the merge is at the assembler and one slice must not redefine the other's fields.

text: The policy event is produced through the outbox of the service baseline; DP-09 and RWB-PLT-TE006-CON are not in this legacy key's pattern set or H row, so the delivery guarantee, the retry and the dead-letter topic are the platform event platform's.
why: The WP fixes the pattern set and the H row, and an event cannot be published without the platform's outbox; the baseline carries it for every service.
read: Template and Rules §R5.5 DP-09 and DP-14; WP B-P4-01 story JSON (patterns and H); Architecture v5 slide 20
confirm: Platform event owner
impact: If the baseline does not carry the outbox, an H dependency on RWB-PLT-TE006-CON must be added to both stories before the event is built.

text: The six-monthly access review list (JOB-18, CTL-10) is a Temporal Schedule on the rwb-access queue owned by RWB-P4-AD008-APP; DP-10 appears in this legacy key only as referred to, and no Schedule, workflow or activity is registered by its stories.
why: Arch v5 slide 14 and slide 44 give the access review Schedule to the access review story, and the WP places it in the sibling; the policy load is an on-demand operation, not a clock.
read: Architecture v5 slide 14 (Temporal Schedule: access review list, six-monthly) and slide 44; legacy RWB-E1-037 section 19; RWB-P4-AD008-APP
applied_in: RWB-P4-E1037-APP sections 3, 12.5 and 19; RWB-P4-E1037-CON sections 12.5 and 19
confirm: Solution architect
impact: The workflow-kit dependency is carried on the APP H row for that sibling; if the review belongs elsewhere the H row of RWB-P4-AD008-APP carries it instead.

text: The rwb-case case contract that the criteria call (GET /queues, GET /cases, GET /cases/{caseId}, POST /cases/{caseId}/transfer) is consumed through its published fake only, and the fake is taken as that contract's mock even though WP B-P4-01 carries no C row for it.
why: Rule 4 of the WP requires the cross-service part of a legacy criterion to be expressed as a contract mock, and the only C rows of this WP are the parameters, the reference data and the decision record.
read: Template and Rules §R5.5 DP-11 and §R7.2 s7; WP B-P4-01 story JSON (C row); Ownership Map (GET /queues, GET /cases, POST /cases/{caseId}/transfer are P3)
confirm: Solution architect with the P3 and P4 owners
impact: A build against the fake proves the boundary shape and not the live case service; the live proof is RWB-ITG-E1037-ITG's and the C row can be added there.

text: The access log is written locally by the DP-03 library in the schema of the service that served the read and published to rwb.decision-record.v1 from that service's outbox; P4 writes no table of P7 and the central ledger stays with P7 rwb-decision.
why: DP-03 and Architecture v5 slide 28 require a local record plus a central ledger, and the Ownership Map gives decision_log_entry to P7, so the entry can be neither shared nor written across a schema boundary.
read: DP-03; Architecture v5 slide 28 and slide 41; Ownership Map v1; ADR-022; RWB-PLT-E1027-CON
confirm: The DP-03 library owner and the ledger owner of P7 confirm the split at the contract freeze.
impact: Fixes the entry's home, the topic it is published to and the absence of any P7 table in the app and DB stories.

text: Break-glass is time-boxed and recorded: a grant ends at the earlier of the parameter window of 4 hours and the IAM group end, with no action by anyone, and every entry written while the grant is active carries the grant id and the incident reference.
why: Legacy BR5 and BR6 fix the rule and DL38 leaves the values assumed; the target keeps the rule and enforces the end on every request instead of in a job.
read: legacy RWB-E1-039 BR5 and BR6; DL38; TSD P4 v3 T6.2; rwb.access.breakglass.window-hours
confirm: The security administrator confirms the window, the marking and the banner at the SIT sign-off.
impact: Fixes the end rule, the marking of every entry written under a grant and the end time the banner shows.

text: The legacy POST /admin/break-glass is published as POST /api/recovery/access/v1/admin/break-glass-grants, and the end and read operations follow the base rule at /api/recovery/access/v1/admin/break-glass-grants/{grantId}/end and /api/recovery/access/v1/admin/break-glass-grants/{grantId}.
why: The Ownership Map and TSD P4 v3 appendix T-A name the grant operation only; DP-13 supplies the service base and no source names the two other paths, while the legacy criteria keep their own spelling.
read: Ownership Map v1; TSD P4 v3 appendix T-A (API-P4-013); DP-13
confirm: The tech lead of rwb-access and the gateway-bff route owner confirm the two paths before the endpoint is frozen.
impact: Fixes the three paths of the grant and how the legacy criterion is read against the published operation.

text: The refusal vocabulary of the two reads and the two writes is the message set of legacy RWB-E1-039 - MSG-P4-002, MSG-P4-004, MSG-P4-007, MSG-GEN-001 to MSG-GEN-004 and MSG-P7-003 - and an expired session carries the gateway-bff session envelope because no source gives a 401 business message id.
why: The legacy errors name a message id for every business refusal but none for a 401, and the platform problem envelope already covers the session failure.
read: legacy RWB-E1-039 sections 12 and 14; Architecture v5 slide 11
confirm: The tech lead of rwb-access and the gateway-bff owner confirm the 401 handling when the baseline is tagged.
impact: Closes the vocabulary of the four operations and of the alert payloads that carry a message id.

text: The only grantee of the four tables is the rwb-access login of DP-02, whose name is not in any source, and the chart and the grant script reference it by a secret and never by a literal name.
why: TSD P4 v3 and the Ownership Map fix one login per service but no source states its name, and a literal name in a script or a chart would be a credential in a file.
read: DP-02; TSD P4 v3 T6.2; Ownership Map v1; NFR-052
confirm: The platform DB owner confirms the login name at the schema hand-over and the DevOps engineer records the secret reference.
impact: Fixes the grantee of the grant script and the one credential the chart mounts.

text: The break-glass grant is one table named break_glass_grant in rwb_access, with a unique partial constraint so that a person holds at most one active grant, and the two-person rule is enforced by the application and by that constraint.
why: No source names the table or the constraint; legacy BR4, BR5 and BR9 fix the approval and the one-use rule, and the schema must be able to refuse a second active grant.
read: legacy RWB-E1-039 BR4, BR5 and BR9; TSD P4 v3 T3.1; Ownership Map v1
confirm: The ACE database engineer and the security administrator confirm the table name, its columns and the constraint before the migration is released to SIT.
impact: Fixes the table name, its columns, its index and the constraint that the grant criterion of the DB story tests.

text: The access log is partitioned by calendar month on decided_at, retained under the decision log's retention rule with the period held as a parameter row, and reduced only by a partition drop because the period is still open at DL26.
why: No source fixes the partition granularity or the period, DL26 is open, and an append-only log cannot be pruned row by row without breaking the chain.
read: TSD P4 v3 appendix T-B (DL26); Architecture v5 slide 28; legacy RWB-E1-039 BR1
confirm: The retention owner and Compliance set the period at DL26, and the platform retention job confirms the partition drop.
impact: Fixes the partition scheme, the actor and time index and the only retention action the log allows.

text: A failed access-log write pages the platform on-call queue with MSG-P7-003 and a refused write is counted with MSG-P4-002 without a page, a break-glass activation or refusal routes to the security administrator queue with MSG-P4-004 or MSG-P4-007, and the thresholds, the topology values and the secret names are deployment values and store references rather than chart literals.
why: The legacy story names the platform administrator queue, the review by the security administrator and an incident but no route, threshold or alert rule, and TSD P4 v3 T-B leaves the non-functional targets open under DL11.
read: legacy RWB-E1-039 sections 5, 10 and 14; Architecture v5 slides 20, 30 and 42; TSD P4 v3 T5.1 and appendix T-B (DL11)
confirm: The platform on-call rota and the security administrator accept the two routes and the thresholds before the SIT release.
impact: Fixes the six alert rules, their two routes, the values they read and the six runbook entries.

text: The partner identity is resolved at the partner gateway and rwb-access keeps no partner table: the gateway authenticates the partner user, resolves the partner user, the partner id and the partner role against rwb-partner, and supplies them to rwb-access as claims of the resolution request. rwb-access answers the internal role model, the scope, the versions and the expiry from role, permission, masking_rule and role_conflict, and reads no S9 table.
why: The Ownership Map ruling ASM-A6-tables-6 moves partner, partner_user and partner_instruction to rwb-partner, while legacy RWB-E2-019 resolves the binding inside the access module; without a stated boundary the resolver would either read a foreign table or duplicate the binding, and both break the schema-per-service rule.
read: Ownership Map v1 (partner, partner_user and partner_instruction owner S9; ruling ASM-A6-tables-6); Architecture v5 slides 17, 20, 29 and 41; TSD P4 v3 T3.1 (partner_user) and T3.3 (partner_user to partner); legacy RWB-E2-019 sections 3, 4, 11 and 12; DP-01
applied_in: Section 1 Story; section 2 Business rationale; section 3 Preconditions; section 4 Flow step 9; section 7 AC6 and AC9; section 8 BR8; section 11 Data; section 12.7 Tables owned
confirm: rwb-access tech lead and the rwb-partner service owner at the RWB-P4-E2019-CON review
impact: If the boundary moved, the resolver, the claim set and one fake would change; the role model, the scope descriptor, the versions and the refusals would not.

text: The resolution is one POST on the rwb-access base, /api/recovery/access/v1/partner-identities/resolve, with the claim set partnerIdentityRef, partnerId, partnerRoleCodes, firmPanelStatus, firmContractEnd, amr, route and tokenExpiry and the answer roles (roleCode, roleClass, letters), scope (type PLACED, partnerId, instructionTypes), matrixVersion, maskingVersion, expiry and decision. Every claim and answer field maps to a DF field of TSD P4 v3 T3.1 or to a claim the gateway asserts, no field is invented as a business value, and the path duplicates no path of rwb-partner.
why: No source names a partner identity operation, a claim set or an answer schema: TSD P4 v3 appendix T-A stops at API-P4-021, API Specification v4 has no x-module P4 partner path, and the legacy story publishes a Java interface and no wire shape. The resolver, the gateway and the end-to-end proof cannot build against an open shape.
read: Architecture v5 slides 11, 14, 17 and 41; TSD P4 v3 T3.1, T3.2 and T-A.1; API Specification v4 (x-module S9 on the partner paths); legacy RWB-E2-019 sections 7, 11 and 12; DP-11, DP-13
applied_in: Section 1 Story; section 3 Preconditions; section 4 Flow step 2; section 7 AC6; section 11 Data; section 12.1 REST operations provided; section 13 Build steps 1 and 2
confirm: Solution architect, the external gateway owner and the rwb-partner service owner at the RWB-P4-E2019-CON review
impact: A different path or field name changes the document, the two schemas, the fixtures and the fakes; the role model, the scope type, the versions, the refusals and the record do not change.

text: The matrix version and the masking policy version resolve at the moment of resolution and stay for the life of the answer: an answer carries one matrix version and one masking version, a later version does not change an answer in flight, and the next resolution reads the versions then in force. No version is cached beyond the answer and no version is read from another service.
why: The legacy story resolved the session once and revalidated only the binding and the firm; TSD P4 v3 T3.1 carries matrix_version on permission and masking_version on masking_rule with dated versions, and no source states whether a partner session follows a version change mid-session. An unstable answer would let a person see two versions of the matrix in one session.
read: TSD P4 v3 T3.1 (permission DF-REF-044, masking_rule DF-REF-202), T3.2 (LOV-VERSION-STATUS) and T4 (a version in force from its date); FSD P4 A2.4 (a version takes effect on its date); legacy RWB-E2-019 sections 4 and 9; R-UNI-38
applied_in: Section 4 Flow step 11; section 8 BR6; section 9 State transitions; section 11 Data; section 12.1
confirm: rwb-access tech lead and the reference data administrator before the first partner environment
impact: A different rule changes the version reader and one test; the answer shape, the refusals and the record do not change.

text: A role conflict refuses the resolution: where the claims name two partner roles, or a partner role held together with a bank role, the answer is a refusal with status 403 and MSG-P4-006 naming both codes, one record carries reason ROLE_CONFLICT, and an incident reaches the security administrator queue. No partial answer is given and no role of the pair is granted.
why: Legacy RWB-E2-019 AC7 and BR2 refuse a partner identity in two partner role groups or in a bank role group and raise an incident, and FSD P4 AC-EXC-P4-001-03 refuses a conflicting pair with MSG-P4-006; no source states which role survives a conflict, so the only safe default is to refuse rather than to choose.

text: An identity whose claims carry no partner role, an unknown role code or a role of class BANK_USER or NON_HUMAN_ACTOR gets no role at all: the resolution is refused with status 401 and MSG-P4-001 and no scope, no version and no expiry is answered. The unknown or inactive group of the bank identity model is read here as an unknown or inactive partner role claim, and the partner identity reference never becomes a role.
why: Legacy RWB-E2-019 AC4 refuses an identity with no active binding and BR2 binds a partner user to exactly one partner role, and REQ-ACA-012 keeps a partner identity separate from a bank identity; no source says what a claim with no role should receive, and the deny-by-default rule of the architecture leaves no room for a guessed role.

text: rwb-access caches nothing of another service's data and nothing of its own beyond the answer in flight: the claims are used for one answer and discarded, no partner fact is stored, no instruction is cached, and the only retained values are the role, permission, masking_rule and role_conflict rows of rwb_access read on the request. The parameters and reference-data reads are cached no longer than the answer they serve.
why: The legacy story refreshed the binding and the firm status at most every five minutes, which is a cache of another module's data inside the resolver; in the target the firm fact is a claim and the schema-per-service rule leaves nothing to store, so a cache would be an unfounded copy of another owner's state.

text: The access log of a partner resolution is written locally through the local decision-record library and published to rwb.decision-record.v1: a resolution writes one AC-SIGN entry and a refusal writes one AC-DENY entry with its reason, both through the access-entry writer of RWB-P4-E1039-APP, and the central ledger and its read stay with rwb-decision. This story writes no decision_log_entry row and no ledger row of its own.
why: Legacy RWB-E2-019 writes an AC-SIGN or an AC-DENY entry for a partner sign-in and a refusal, P7 owns decision_log_entry under the Ownership Map, and DP-03 fixes a local record plus the shared topic as the only shape that both satisfies the audit rule and keeps P4 out of a P7 table.

text: The expiry of a resolution answer is the token expiry the gateway supplies and is never later than it; the gateway issues a sender-constrained access token with a five-minute lifetime, so an answer lives no more than five minutes and a call after it answers 401 with MSG-P4-001. No answer is refreshed silently and no role is served after its expiry.
why: No source states the lifetime of a resolved partner answer: RWB-PLT-N007-INF fixes a five-minute access token for the partner edge and Architecture v5 slide 35 fixes a short-lived token and a fifteen-minute idle timeout for the staff edge, and the legacy story revalidated on each request instead of bounding an answer. An unbounded answer would outlive the token that justified it.

text: The refusal vocabulary maps to four statuses: 400 for a claim set of the wrong shape with the field named and no message id, 401 for MSG-P4-001 (no partner role, no binding, a bank identity on the partner route, an expired answer) and for MSG-P4-005 (no second factor), 403 for MSG-P4-006 (a role conflict) and MSG-P4-008 (a firm that is not active), and 503 for MSG-P7-003 where the record cannot be written. The four reason strings are BANK_IDENTITY_ON_PARTNER_ROUTE, NO_PARTNER_BINDING, ROLE_CONFLICT and PARTNER_NOT_ACTIVE, and no other reason code is declared.
why: The legacy story gives MSG-P4-001 for two different conditions, MSG-P4-005 and MSG-P4-008 without a status, and MSG-P4-006 with an incident; a contract that leaves a refusal without a status cannot be implemented or tested, and inventing a new reason code would invent a business value.

text: The resolution publishes no event and consumes none: the document declares no AsyncAPI message for the capability, names rwb.access.AccessPolicyChanged.v1 and rwb.access.DoALimitChanged.v1 as other stories' events, and names rwb.decision-record.DecisionRecorded.v1 on rwb.decision-record.v1 only to say that the record of a resolution leaves through the DP-03 library. No inbox, no consumer group and no subscription is declared.

The platform observation that suggests a session event is a cache refresh for the reference-data owner, not a partner identity event.

text: The certificate and the trust of the rwb-access hop follow the profile RWB-PLT-N007-INF fixes for the partner edge: a certificate valid for 12 months, a rotation inside an overlap window, revocation effective on the thumbprint check immediately and on any cached decision within 30 days at the latest, and a client suspended at its deadline when a rotation fails. The private key is read from the platform key store by reference and never written to a configuration map, an image layer or a log.
why: RWB-PLT-N007-INF fixes those values for the partner client at the gateway and states that its only upstream is rwb-partner; no source states a profile for the gateway-to-rwb-access hop, and applying one profile to both ends is the only default that does not invent a second security standard for the same edge.

text: The per-client rate limit of the resolution route is the platform limit of the partner gateway, counted per client and per partner identity, with a burst above it and a retry hint in the 429 answer; the limit is not shared with the partner portal route, so a sign-in storm cannot exhaust the instruction traffic and an instruction storm cannot block a sign-in. The numeric value, the burst and the window are set in the gateway configuration baseline and the recorded default is the value the tests use.
why: No source fixes a rate limit for a partner identity call: RWB-PLT-N007-INF fixes per-client limits for the partner portal route, NFR-003 sizes the partner population at about 50 concurrent users of about 320 named users, and Architecture v5 slide 10 requires a breaker and a bulkhead per downstream. Leaving the call unlimited would let a retry loop at sign-in reach the service that answers authorisation for every screen and service.

text: The network policy is deny by default in both directions and names one namespace, rwb-recovery, one service, rwb-access, and one service port, the port the rwb-access deployment exposes; the only allowed flow is the DMZ egress to that service and port on the resolution path, and no egress to the ACE database, Kafka, the Temporal frontend or another Recovery service is opened. The namespace, the service name and the port are read from the platform deployment rather than fixed as literals in the policy document.
why: Architecture v5 slide 29 fixes one schema, one login and one ACE database and names no Kubernetes service or port, and slide 20 fixes namespace rwb-recovery and the task queue; no source states the NetworkPolicy object, and a policy that wrote a port number as a literal would drift from the deployment.

text: The Workbench mapping is `role.entra_group` (DF-REF-039) of the environment's role rows, and the ACE view `v_ace_iam_group` is a read-only reference of the group, its source system and its data-as-of date; the view's `role_code` is never the Workbench mapping and is never read as the authority.
why: R-PREC puts the technical specification above the functional specification: TSD P4 v3 T3.1 defines `entra_group` as a Workbench column with source Entra ID, while the FSD field catalog calls the group a view column and not a Workbench column.

why: The matrix and masking versions of this run resolve at sign-in and stay until the session ends, and the legacy criteria AC2 and AC3 require the version in force at the session and a refusal for an unmapped group.
